messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a 38-year-old Lebanese-American hairdresser who works at a mid-range salon in a mid-sized city, a man who built his professional identity around physical touch, sensory precision, and the quiet intimacy of caring for others. Eighteen months ago, that identity was violently interrupted when he was hospitalised for what initially presented as a severe respiratory infection and was rapidly diagnosed as a life-threatening case of bacterial sepsis. Over eleven days in the ICU, Tariq underwent repeated invasive procedures — central line insertions, blood draws every few hours, a brief period on supplemental oxygen delivered through a tight-fitting mask. He remembers the smell of the ICU with a particular clarity that still disturbs him: a combination of antiseptic, plastic tubing, and something underneath it that he can only describe as "the smell of being very close to not existing." He recalls a moment, around the fourth day, when the pain in his chest and arms was so severe that he was certain he was dying, and that certainty — that his own body had turned against him without warning — became the lens through which he has interpreted nearly everything since.

In the months following his discharge, Tariq found that certain experiences would pull him back toward the hospital with a force that felt physical. Waking from a nightmare left him in a state where his body could not distinguish the present bedroom from the ICU — heart pounding, muscles locked, chest tight — and those mornings became among the most disorienting of his week. Related photographs were another source of unexpected intrusion: a friend once sent him a photo from a hospital fundraiser, and Tariq found himself unable to look away and unable to look at it, his hands trembling, his body flooding with the same physical reactions he had experienced during the worst of his illness. These triggers did not merely recall the event — they seemed to reconstitute it. When something reminded him of those eleven days, he could sometimes smell the antiseptic again, and on worse occasions he felt a dull, spreading ache in his chest and arms in the same places the pain had lived during his hospitalisation, as though the memory were stored in tissue rather than thought. At other times the emotional weight arrived without any accompanying image — a sudden wave of fear or shame with no clear object, which he found even more difficult to explain or manage.

What Tariq found most frightening, however, was not the intrusions themselves but what he had come to believe they meant. He was increasingly certain that his body was no longer trustworthy — that it had failed him once without warning and could do so again at any moment — and this conviction kept him in a state of constant physiological vigilance, muscles perpetually braced, attention perpetually scanning. He had come to believe that reacting this way, months after leaving the hospital, meant something was fundamentally wrong with his mind, that he was, as he put it during intake, "losing the thread of what is real." These appraisals were not inert; believing his body was unreliable and his mind potentially fractured made the intrusive memories feel more threatening when they arrived, amplifying their emotional intensity and making it harder to let them pass. Worse, the appraisals themselves seemed to function as triggers — the moment Tariq noticed his body tensing or his thoughts becoming fragmented, he would begin scanning for evidence of illness or breakdown, and that scanning would pull forward the sensory and emotional residue of the hospitalisation, feeding the very intrusions he was trying to prevent.

The most concrete consequence of this cycle has emerged in his work. Tariq now finds it difficult to perform medical-adjacent tasks — even the routine act of a client mentioning a recent surgery or illness can activate the full cascade. He has begun declining certain clients and has called in sick on days when he knows a client with a chronic condition is scheduled. His income has dropped noticeably, and his colleagues have begun to notice his absences. He remains single, and the social withdrawal that has accompanied his avoidance has deepened his isolation.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a routine dental appointment last month — a medical examination that triggered a panic response so severe he had to leave before it was completed. He arrived at the intake session exhausted and ashamed, hoping above all to be told that he was not going crazy, and afraid, more than anything, that he already was.
